I am not a vegetarian, but, let's be serious, experts have been telling us for years, we need to eat less meat. Probably the healthiest polenta yogurt is made from millet and black baluga lentils. You can easily grow both in your garden. (Polenta yogurt can also be made, for instance, from corn and garbanzo beans, or from brown rice and mung beans.) The ratio is 2 parts millet to one part lentil. This is not really a recipe but to visualize, lets say 2/3 cup millet and 1/3 cup black lentil. Millet is my go to because it has no phytic acid and no lectins. Black lentil is probably the least inflammatory and least toxic, and most nutritious bean on earth. It is one of the very few proteins that is alkaline. Eaten together they make a "complementary protein" which means the amount of protein that your body actually assimilates and uses is just about doubles. This combination basically fools your digestive system into thinking it is meat. And bite for bite it has as much high quality protein as meat.

Sprouting greatly reduces both the starches and the phytic acid, increases the amount of protein, and it releases vitamins, enzymes and phytochemicals. Millet seed has about 40 grams of net carbohydrate per serving, and the lentils have about 7 grams of protein per serving. We sprout both for three days. Due to sprouting, the net carbs in the millet goes down to about 20. And the protein in the black lentils goes up to 26 -- yes, you read that right, it goes from 7 to 26 --which is slightly better than soy bean. We put both sprouts in a blender and add 4 cups of water, and blend on high speed until it is a smooth batter. We then pour it into a bowl, and put the bown in a pressure cooker, and pressure cook it on high for 20 minutes. We now have cooked polenta. If you wanted to you could eat it, right now, as is.

Note: Sprouting and pressure cooking beans and seeds breaks down phytic acid, lectins, the anti nutrients -- including the things that cause us to "pass wind". You would be amazed at how much better it makes garbazo beans taste.

Here is how the rest of the new magic happens. We let the polenta cool down to 135 degrees F and innoculate it with a well known Japanese probiotic called non alcoholic Amazake Koji (which I will talk about in the next paragraph) and we let the polenta ferment at 135 degrees (using the keep warm function on a cheep rice cooker), for five to eight hours. The amazake koji converts all starches into simple sugars. If you were to taste it at this point it would taste quite sweet -- like someone had added five tablespoons of sugar. Aut Amazake koji does more than just convert starches to sugar. It creates the perfect environment for yogurt bacteria to grow and thrive. Using koji to prepare the "milk" is the best way I have found to make non dairy yougurt. We then reduce the temperature to 110 degrees F, which is what happens when you put your millet/black lentil polinta into a yogurt maker. And we add non dairy yogurt starter. At some point you can add a few tablespoons of MCT oil for "mouth feel" if you want. We let this yogurt incubate for up to 8 hours. As it progresses it develops a delightful sweet and sour flavor. You keep sampling once in a while. When you like how it tastes, you are done. Like all yogurt, you put it in the refrigerator and let it cool.

You have just made millet/black lentil polenta yogurt. One of the coolest things about it is complex carbohydrates, fiber, and resistant starches in the millet and lentils still remain in the yogurt. All that is missing is the sugar and starch. If you let the yogurt ferment until it is completely sour, it is probably is OK for someone to eat who is on a Keto diet to eat. I am on one and it works for me.

Koji. The sophisticated people of Japan have been exploring and using Koji for at least a thousand years. It is what they use to make soy sauce, miso, natto, sake and so much more. We picked the strand they use to make what they call Amazake Koji. This ferment makes a very sweet desert pudding by converting the starch in cooked white rice to sugar.

Here is a YouTube on Amazake Koji: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9rbY3idc790

I use a fancy multipot that does everything. But if you are going to use a stove top pressure cooker, you will probably also need a cheep rice cooker (for the first incubation), and a yogurt maker (for the second incubation) -- or the equivalent. I prefer my multipot to a stovetop pressure cooker because it is programmable and safer, makes no noise, and does not fill my tiny house with steam. The steam stays inside the multipot.

You can eat the poleta yogurt as yogurt, by the spoonful, or treat it like a sour dough starter, add flour and make bread. I add almond, coconut, or cauliflower flour to make gludten free, keto friendly bread, bagels, pizza, or whatever. You can add concentrated leaf protein, with sausage seasonings and turn it into sausage; and you can make really good tasting non dairy cheese from it too. There are so many things you can do with this. I am writing a cook book on this too. But thought I would share it with you tonight.

You can order koji from highly skilled artisans over the internet, or imported from Japan through Amazon, as well as yougurt starter, and if you want to, it is even possible to make your own. There are many good books on it. Amazake Koji may be a new concept for some people, but it is not new to quite a few Americans or to anyone living in or coming from Japan. My polenta yogurt tastes good, is filling, is full of protein, you can make it from out of your own garden, and, oh ya, it also happens to be good for you. God Bless. Over and Out.
